facts.title: Discovered Three Times Over
facts.text: Oxygen was isolated independently by Carl Wilhelm Scheele in Sweden around 1771-1772 and by Joseph Priestley in England in 1774, but Priestley published first. It was Antoine Lavoisier in France who recognized it as a true element and explained its role in combustion, demolishing the old phlogiston theory. His insight reshaped chemistry into a quantitative science.

facts.title: A Name That Means Acid-Maker
facts.text: Lavoisier coined the name 'oxygène' in 1777 from the Greek words 'oxys' (sharp or acid) and 'genes' (producer), because he wrongly believed oxygen was an essential ingredient of all acids. We now know hydrogen, not oxygen, is the defining element of acids. The mistaken name stuck and is still used worldwide today.

facts.title: The Most Abundant Element on Earth
facts.text: By mass, oxygen makes up about 46% of Earth's crust, making it the most abundant element in the rocks beneath our feet. It is locked into silicate minerals, oxides, and water rather than floating free as gas. Oxygen is also the third most abundant element in the entire universe, forged inside massive stars.

facts.title: It Turns Liquids Pale Blue
facts.text: When cooled to about -183 degrees Celsius, oxygen condenses into a pale sky-blue liquid, and it freezes into a bluish solid near -219 degrees. This faint color comes from the way oxygen molecules absorb red light. Liquid oxygen is also magnetic and will visibly cling to the poles of a strong magnet.

facts.title: The Air We Cannot Live Without
facts.text: Oxygen makes up roughly 21% of the air by volume, the precise level our bodies are tuned to. In our cells, it serves as the final electron acceptor in respiration, allowing mitochondria to extract energy from food efficiently. Without it, complex animal life as we know it could not exist.

facts.title: Photosynthesis Filled the Sky
facts.text: Earth's early atmosphere had almost no free oxygen until cyanobacteria began producing it through photosynthesis billions of years ago. This triggered the Great Oxidation Event around 2.4 billion years ago, transforming the planet's chemistry and rusting the oceans' dissolved iron. Nearly all the oxygen we breathe today is a byproduct of living organisms.

facts.title: Ozone, Oxygen's Protective Cousin
facts.text: Three oxygen atoms can bond into ozone (O3), a pale blue gas with a sharp smell you may notice after a thunderstorm. High in the stratosphere, the ozone layer absorbs most of the Sun's harmful ultraviolet radiation, shielding life below. At ground level, however, ozone is a pollutant that can damage lungs and crops.

facts.title: The Engine of Combustion and Rust
facts.text: Oxygen does not burn itself, but it powerfully supports burning by reacting with fuels to release heat and light. The same chemistry, running slowly, causes iron to rust and apples to brown. Industries exploit this by blasting pure oxygen into steel furnaces, where it rapidly removes carbon impurities from molten iron.

facts.title: A Lifesaver in Medicine
facts.text: Medical oxygen is one of the most widely used treatments in hospitals, given to patients with pneumonia, severe asthma, or low blood oxygen. Liquid oxygen also fuels rockets, including the engines that powered the Saturn V and the Space Shuttle. Most industrial oxygen is produced by chilling and distilling ordinary air into its components.

facts.title: Three Isotopes Tell Earth's Story
facts.text: Natural oxygen comes mostly as oxygen-16, with tiny amounts of oxygen-17 and oxygen-18. Scientists measure the ratio of these isotopes trapped in ancient ice cores and seashells to reconstruct past climates. Because heavier oxygen-18 evaporates less easily, its abundance acts as a natural thermometer reaching back hundreds of thousands of years.
